fact: Tom Allen began fighting at about twenty years old, around 1860 to 1861.
Tom Allen fought 23 battles between 1860 and 1879.
Tom Allen had fought thirteen hard battles in England, beginning in 1861.
Tom Allen and Mike McCoole made pugilistic affairs very lively in the West after the Civil War.
After vainly challenging Mace, Tom Allen claimed the British heavyweight title, but Mace kept the belt.
After beating Davis in January 1869, Tom Allen claimed the championship of America.
Tom Allen claimed to be the English champion of the prize ring in early 1869.
The Republic gave Tom Allen's fighting weight as 164 pounds in June 1869.
Tom Allen was called champion of America, of the United States or of the prize ring through 1869 and early 1870.
Tom Allen trained in Cincinnati in autumn 1869, at the Buckeye House under Jim Coyne and Earl.
By about 1870 Tom Allen was at the front of pugilists in America.
Tom Allen held the championship from 1870 until 1876 and was eager to regain it.
St. Louis friends presented Tom Allen with a championship belt at the Theater Comique on 30 April 1870.
Tom Allen fought Jem Mace in May 1870.
Tom Allen issued a challenge in May 1870 signed 'Champion of America, by permission of James Mace, champion of the world'.
Tom Allen was introduced as champion of America at Tammany in June 1870.
Tom Allen announced his retirement from the prize ring in November 1870.
Tom Allen had appeared before the public seventeen times as a prize fighter.
Tom Allen's card read 'Tom Allen, Champion, St. Louis'.
Tom Allen was described as an Englishman of about 170 pounds, lately champion around 1873.
Tom Allen beat Mike McCoole on 23 September 1873, regaining the heavyweight title.
At a benefit on 25 September 1873, manager Fred Wilson introduced Tom Allen as the champion of the world.
Tom Allen was described as the celebrated young champion in November 1873.
In early 1874 Tom Allen claimed to be champion of America.
Tom Allen announced his retirement from the ring in November 1874 and did not intend to enter it that year.
Tom Allen said in February 1875 that he would no longer fight in the roped arena.
In March 1875 Tom Allen was called champion of America, by the New York Sun and in an inscription on a goblet presented to him.
Tom Allen announced in June 1875 that he was withdrawing from the ring for good and would make no more matches.
In January 1876 Tom Allen of St. Louis was described as holding the title of champion of America.
In February 1876 Tom Allen said he had retired from the ring only until an opportunity came to get back in.
In May 1876 Tom Allen weighed 195 pounds and expected to reduce to his fighting weight of about 178 pounds within twelve weeks.
In September 1876 Tom Allen lost the championship of America to Joe Goss in his last battle.

In September 1876 Tom Allen announced his withdrawal from the ring in cards published in the Cincinnati evening papers, saying he would never enter it again and would become a private citizen after his benefit.
The Post-Dispatch called Tom Allen the champion of the squared circle in September 1876 and said he was with them in St. Louis.
In October 1876 the Theatre Comique advertised Tom Allen and Jem Mace as the Two Champions of the World.
In September 1877 Tom Allen was described as the champion of America.
In March 1878 Tom Allen was described as the Champion of America.
Tom Allen won the championship of England in 1878 by beating Charles Davis, and the paper called him the champion pugilist.
On 22 May 1878 in London, Tom Allen was presented with a silver cup inscribed as champion boxer of England by his backers and admirers.
In June 1879 Tom Allen claimed that Dwyer could not claim the championship until he met Allen in the ring, since Allen had kept a challenge open to the world and had won the title three times.
A 1903 article gives 1880 as the year Tom Allen started his career as a fighter.
A 1934 article says Tom Allen was heavyweight champion in the 1880s.
A silver cup inscribed as champion boxer of England was on display at Patsy Sheppard's in October 1882.
In November 1882 Tom Allen was said to have won more battles than any other man in England.
From 1882 to 1883 the press described Tom Allen as an ex-prize fighter or ex-champion.
Tom Allen returned to St. Louis from England in December 1882 and received a cordial welcome at St. Louis sporting resorts.
In December 1882 Tom Allen said he preferred bare-fist fighting to hard or soft gloves.
On 27 January 1883 The Republic described Tom Allen as the late world's champion when he came to the stage at the Muldoon-Bauer match.
From 1886 to 1889 the press described Tom Allen as the ex-champion, or the retired champion pugilist, of the world.
Tom Allen advertised himself as the retired champion pugilist of the world in newspaper advertisements from February to December 1890.
Tom Allen advertised himself as the retired champion pugilist of the world in newspaper advertisements from January to December 1891.
Tom Allen was advertised as, and styled himself, the retired champion pugilist of the world during 1892.
Tom Allen was advertised as the retired champion pugilist of the world during 1893.
Tom Allen was described and advertised as a retired champion of the world from 1894 into 1895, and signed a December 1894 letter as "Retired Champion of the World".
A saloon cup Tom Allen won from Charles Davis in 1878 was kept behind the bar of his saloon in a glass case in 1895.
Tom Allen was advertised as the retired champion pugilist of the world from June 1896 to March 1897.
Tom Allen was billed in advertisements and described in print as the retired champion pugilist of the world from 1898 to 1900.
In March and April 1903 Tom Allen was described as a retired champion pugilist living in St. Louis.
An estate inventory of Tom Allen's property, dated July 1903, listed a champion's cup.
